articles.title: Arquivos do Céu: série do Globoplay trata sobre OVNIs em São José | G1
articles.standfirst: Caso no Vale do Paraíba aconteceu há 40 anos e, até hoje, é um mistério. Produção também trás outros fenômenos ufológicos do Brasil.
articles.summary: Caso no Vale do Paraíba aconteceu há 40 anos e, até hoje, é um mistério. Produção também trás outros fenômenos ufológicos do Brasil.
articles.body:
O mistério da Noite dos OVNIs, fenômeno que mobilizou caças da Força Aérea Brasileira (FAB) em São José dos Campos , no interior de São Paulo, há 40 anos, é um dos casos retratados na nova série documental do Globoplay, "Arquivos do Céu", lançada nesta quinta-feira (29).

A série traz relatos inéditos sobre a Noite dos OVNIs, incluindo o depoimento do controlador de voo que acompanhou o caso e rompe o silêncio pela primeira vez. A produção também apresenta a história de um fotógrafo que afirma ter tido os negativos de suas imagens levados misteriosamente para os Estados Unidos.

Em entrevista ao g1 , o diretor da produção, Caio Cavechini, contou os bastidores das gravações, os desafios de investigar relatos de avistamentos e como a equipe buscou reunir diferentes perspectivas sobre um dos episódios ufológicos mais famosos do Brasil.

A série tem cinco episódios e revisita casos conhecidos da ufologia brasileira, com relatos de testemunhas, investigações e personagens ligados a fenômenos que permanecem sem explicação definitiva.

"As histórias de avistamentos são preciosas, merecem ser contadas. Seus detalhes são ricos, ainda que muitas vezes não comprováveis. Cruzamos relatos, buscamos relações e aproximações com outros casos e outras hipóteses", afirma Cavechini.

Segundo o diretor, a proposta foi construir uma narrativa que reunisse diferentes pontos de vista sobre os fenômenos, incluindo o de ufólogos, cientistas e testemunhas.

"E nos apoiamos em um narrador diferente, o Lulu Santos, dono de uma voz capaz de transitar entre o mistério, a filosofia e o humor leve. Nossa aposta foi por criar um documentário diverso e surpreendente, abarcando os ufólogos, os cientistas, as testemunhas e muitos mais", conta.

Noite dos ovnis reprodução do jornal Valeparaibano — Foto: Arquivo pessoal/Adenir Britto

A Noite dos OVNIs aconteceu em 19 de maio de 1986 e ficou marcada por relatos de objetos voadores não identificados observados nos céus de diferentes estados brasileiros.

Ao menos 21 objetos foram relatados em São Paulo, Rio de Janeiro, Minas Gerais e Goiás. O episódio mobilizou a Força Aérea Brasileira, que enviou cinco caças para tentar interceptar os alvos.

Segundo relatos da época, os objetos mudavam de posição em alta velocidade e desapareciam dos radares. Nenhum dos caças enviados conseguiu alcançá-los.

Noite dos OVNIs: diretor revela bastidores de série do Globoplay com relato inédito sobre mistério de 40 anos no interior de SP — Foto: Reprodução/Globoplay

O caso começou quando o operador da torre do Aeroporto de São José dos Campos avistou pontos luminosos que mudavam de cor. Ele questionou o piloto Alcir Pereira, que também confirmou ter visto as luzes.

O empresário e engenheiro aeronáutico Ozires Silva, um dos fundadores da Embraer, foi outra testemunha importante. Na época, presidente da Petrobras, ele pilotava um avião executivo que seguia de Brasília para São José dos Campos quando relatou ter observado luzes misteriosas acompanhando a aeronave.

De acordo com registros do Ministério da Justiça e da Aeronáutica, os objetos foram monitorados por radares em diferentes estados.

Um relatório assinado pelo brigadeiro José Pessoa Cavalcanti Albuquerque apontou que os fenômenos observados "são sólidos e refletem de certa forma inteligência", em referência à capacidade de acompanhar aeronaves e voar em formação. O documento só foi divulgado oficialmente em 2009, 23 anos depois do episódio.

Para Caio Cavechini, um dos desafios da produção foi aproximar perspectivas diferentes sobre os fenômenos ufológicos, incluindo as explicações científicas e os relatos de quem afirma ter presenciado avistamentos.

"A ufologia tem grande resistência por parte dos cientistas. E mesmo assim é um campo bastante popular, tanto pelos mais entusiastas, quanto pelos curiosos. E o nosso desafio era aproximar esses dois campos, incluindo argumentos e narrativas de ambos os lados", explica.

O diretor afirma que a equipe procurou ouvir as pessoas sem julgamentos, inclusive aquelas que não conseguiram encontrar uma explicação para o que dizem ter presenciado.

"É preciso dizer que mesmo os cientistas mais céticos narram episódios de avistamento que não conseguem explicar. Então fomos a campo ouvir, sem julgamentos", diz.

Documentos confidenciais divulgados pela FAB — Foto: Arquivo Nacional

Com cinco episódios, "Arquivos do Céu" também aborda outros casos conhecidos, como a Operação Prato, investigação realizada no Pará que apurou relatos de fenômenos luminosos e supostos ataques a moradores.

A produção acompanha investigações sobre avistamentos de supostos extraterrestres e apresenta novos personagens e informações relacionados a episódios ufológicos no Brasil e no exterior.

O primeiro episódio da série está disponível no Globoplay também para quem não é assinante da plataforma.

Segundo Cavechini, mesmo décadas depois dos acontecimentos, as testemunhas continuam se lembrando dos episódios com riqueza de detalhes.

"Mesmo décadas depois de terem presenciado esses fenômenos misteriosos, as pessoas continuam se lembrando, com riqueza de detalhes, de tudo o que viveram. E isso não é exclusividade de quem está no documentário. Mesmo pessoas com quem conversamos informalmente, durante a produção, ainda guardam essas memórias. Inclusive o Lulu Santos", conclui o diretor.

articles.title: Novembro deve ter mais chuva no RS, mas sem previsão de calor extremo | G1
articles.standfirst: Climatempo Meteorologia indica que a combinação entre maior presença de nuvens, ocorrência constante de chuva e eventuais incursões de ar frio deve impedir que as temperaturas disparem.
articles.summary: Climatempo indica que a combinação entre maior presença de nuvens, ocorrência constante de chuva e eventuais incursões de ar frio deve impedir que as temperaturas disparem.
articles.body:
Chuva em Porto Alegre — Foto: Ronaldo Bernardi/ Grupo RBS

O Rio Grande do Sul deve enfrentar mais um mês marcado pela chuva frequente em novembro .

A previsão da Climatempo Meteorologia indica volumes acima da média para o estado , cenário influenciado pela atuação persistente do El Niño , que segue com forte intensidade e continua alterando os padrões climáticos no país.

Além do excesso de precipitação, o mês também deve ter temperaturas mais amenas do que o habitual para esta época do ano . Embora os dias quentes voltem a ocorrer com mais frequência em relação a outubro, a expectativa é de que o estado não registre períodos prolongados de calor intenso .

Segundo a previsão, a combinação entre maior presença de nuvens, ocorrência constante de chuva e eventuais incursões de ar frio deve impedir que as temperaturas disparem. Com isso, os termômetros tendem a se manter próximos ou ligeiramente abaixo da média para novembro.

O fenômeno El Niño continua sendo o principal fator por trás das condições climáticas previstas para o Sul do país . Neste ano, o aquecimento das águas do Pacífico Equatorial tem provocado mudanças na circulação atmosférica sobre a América do Sul, favorecendo a passagem de sistemas que estimulam a formação de chuva.

🔥 O El Niño é um fenômeno climático natural que ocorre em intervalos irregulares, geralmente a cada 2 a 7 anos. Ele é caracterizado pelo aquecimento maior ou igual a 0,5ºC das águas superficiais do Oceano Pacífico Equatorial. Esse aquecimento altera a circulação dos ventos e a distribuição de calor e umidade ao redor do globo, impactando os padrões de clima em diversas partes do mundo .

Segundo a Climatempo, há ainda a possibilidade de formação da Zona de Convergência do Atlântico Sul (ZCAS) durante a primeira quinzena de novembro. O sistema é conhecido por organizar grandes áreas de instabilidade e pode reforçar os episódios de chuva em diferentes regiões do país .

Apesar da tendência de temperaturas mais comportadas no Sul, novembro seguirá sendo um mês tipicamente quente no Brasil.

articles.title: Who are the real winners of The Celebrity Traitors? Miranda Hart, King Kenny and Maya Jama stand out
articles.summary: Certain stars have been tipped by industry experts as getting the biggest career boost after the show.
articles.body:
Spoiler warning: This article reveals details from The Celebrity Traitors final

In some ways, all the players on the Celebrity Traitors can be seen as winners.

They all got to appear on a hugely popular TV show, rubbing shoulders with other stars and gaining new fans along the way.

But there are certain celebrities, such as Miranda Hart , King Kenny , Maya Jama and Joanne McNally , who have been tipped by industry experts as getting the biggest career boost after the show.

Sebastian "Bash" Croft - who won the game, alongside Romesh Ranganathan - could also now be in line for greater roles.

We've taken a look at the breakout stars of the series and what might lie ahead for them.

After a spell of ill-health, the show has done wonders for bringing Miranda Hart back into the public eye.

There was that incredible “Little Mix Big Mix” viral dance moment, but Hart also displayed a level of vulnerability which stood out in a show where the stars don't really talk about their personal lives.

When her friend Joe Lycett was banished, her tearful reaction to his exit provided a rare poignant moment.

"Connection and laughter and joy are bigger than this game - and to meet someone and just play and laugh, it's all us humans need, you know?" she said.

When she was murdered, she also demonstrated genuine emotion in her response. "Ultimately, in my little personal story, this has been quite extraordinary," she said.

For culture journalist Natalie Jamieson, Hart's openness and relatability made her the "standout" star from this year's series.

And it could also lead to us seeing more of Hart on the small screen. According to The Sun , the BBC is looking to bring back her self-titled sitcom after her stint on Celebrity Traitors led to fresh interest in the show.

The BBC declined to comment on the possible return of Hart’s show.

But she’s not the only one who won hearts by showing real warmth.

The same could be said for Romesh Ranganathan - who, in a departure from his usual cynical, deadpan stand-up persona, seemed really to care about his fellow cast members. Jerry Hall also won viewers over with her charming eccentricity.

And then there’s James Acaster , who showed genuine vulnerability as he struggled to come to terms with being a traitor.

Social media users seemed split after his bombshell confession to being a traitor , with some totally exasperated and others saying they respected him for going out on his own terms.

Either way, he's definitely got the nation talking.

When it comes to celebrities who are most likely to see the biggest career boost, most experts say Kenny is King.

Going into the castle, the 29-year-old was best known to younger fans as a member of the popular British YouTube collective Beta Squad.

But Kenny will have been "the least familiar name to a mainstream audience," says showbiz journalist Nikki Onafuye.

That all changed as he was recruited as a traitor, bringing much-needed energy to the turret - and he made it all the way through to Friday night’s tense final .

Having shown he can hold his own alongside established broadcasters, actors and comedians, big things could now be in store for Kenny.

"He 100% has just been minted as a mainstream star now," said Marina Hyde, on The Rest is Entertainment podcast.

“The next steps could be panel shows, presenting roles, reality competitions or entertainment formats,” adds TV reporter Siobhan Synnot.

Fellow traitor Maya Jama also sailed all the way to the final with her cool-as-a-cucumber persona making her a traitor to be reckoned with.

Despite being banished in dramatic fashion, she could now be in line to receive £1m per deal, according to a report in The Times earlier this week .

What Celebrity Traitors has done for Jama is allow her to reveal more of her personality than on Love Island, says Onafuye.

But TV reporter Synnot thinks between the two, Kenny has more to gain because he has introduced himself to millions of new viewers - whereas Jama was already one of Britain's best-known TV presenters before Celebrity Traitors.

"Maya's gain is subtler: she can emerge looking less like the presenter of Love Island and more like a genuinely versatile television star," she says.

Of all the comedians in the castle, Joanne McNally was initially the least well known, says Caroline Frost, TV editor at Radio Times.

But she flourished on the show, lasting right up to Thursday's semi-final.

"And she's taken her own path, ignoring the herd and making her own voting decisions, sometimes chaotically, but always with charm, wit and good humour,” says Frost.

The Irish comedian's podcast was already popular before the show.

But after her stint as the joker of the pack, bigger things could now lie in store for her.

Just a few days ago, it was announced that her stand-up tour has been extended into 2027, "due to phenomenal demand".

And her agents will be "fielding calls" for her to bring her star power to other shows, adds Frost.

Culture journalist Jamieson says some of the other female contestants - such as Sharon Rooney , Leigh-Anne Pinnock and Myha'la - also stood out for showing their wit and wisdom, which could serve them well in the outside world.

Things got a bit awkward in one of the episodes , when Sharon disagreed with some of the cast on a challenge, with some social media users saying she was acting in a "childish" way.

But others argued it was a classic case of women being drowned out by men.

"There's been a subtlety in the smartness of women on display here, alongside the frustration of not always being listened to in the game," says Jamieson.

In the end, it was faithful duo Romesh Ranganathan and Sebastian ‘Bash’ Croft who emerged victorious.

Comedian Ranganathan was already a huge star, but the show has introduced Croft, 24, to a much wider audience.

He’s had previous acting roles in Game of Thrones and Heartstopper , but Traitors allowed him to show his own personality, "which as we've seen has endeared him both to other players and the huge watching audience", says Frost.

He is also building his career as a pop star, and he's had a strong presence on social media during the series, posting videos of his tracks.

His debut EP comes out later in November, perfect timing to capitalise on his Traitors win.

What's clear is that the true victors aren't necessarily the ones who get their hands on the prize pot.

Arguably, what matters most is the amount of screen time you get - and what you do with it.

On that note, spare a thought for those who left the show early, such as Amol Rajan , Julie Hesmondhalgh and Hannah Fry .

But all made an impact in their own way and, as Synnot points out, they get "a nice anecdote" for future interviews.

And what of James Blunt , who stole hearts with his military approach to the challenges and eccentric Top Gun-style outfits - and who came so close to winning the whole show?

Maybe he's the mystery man in contention for the new James B(ond) - although his hapless theories could mean he'll be in line to be the new Johnny English instead.

articles.title: 'Politicisation of energy flows harmful': Jaishankar calls for diversified supply chains at G20
articles.summary: External affairs minister S Jaishankar on Saturday called for reducing political interference in energy markets and diversifying global supply chains,
articles.body: External affairs minister S Jaishankar on Saturday called for reducing political interference in energy markets and diversifying global supply chains, saying disruptions were placing a disproportionate burden on developing countries.Speaking about the message he delivered at G20 foreign ministers' meeting in Atlanta, Jaishankar said the discussions covered geopolitical conflicts, energy and food security, and resilient supply chains.“Look, there are big conflicts today, two major conflicts which are having global ramifications,” ANI quoted him as saying. He added that “there are no military solutions; we have to find a diplomatic pathway.”On energy security, Jaishankar warned against disruptions in fuel distribution and their impact on developing economies. “This distortion of the energy markets, the politicisation of energy flows, this is something which is very harmful,” he said, adding that “the Global South was bearing the brunt of the energy shortages and that something needs to be done.”He also flagged risks to food security, citing disruptions to grain shipments through the Black Sea and fertiliser shortages linked to tensions in the Persian Gulf and Red Sea regions.At the meeting's concluding session on supply chains, Jaishankar called for wider diversification of manufacturing and production across countries. “Today we need more diversified supply chains,” he said, advocating “more globalised, you know, more diversified production, more diversified manufacturing.”In a post on X after the session, he said securing supply chains was central to the global economy's well-being and called on the G20 to promote “the right to industrialise” and resist “predatory practices”.“Diversification and de-risking, including in connectivity, is the key to supply chain resilience, threatened by pandemics, conflicts, climate events and mishaps,” he said.Jaishankar also urged the grouping to work towards the “de-politicisation of markets” and prevent the concentration of production and resources in a few geographies.US secretary of state Marco Rubio, who hosted the meeting, also stressed the need to secure critical trade routes, including the Strait of Hormuz and the Bab el-Mandeb, and strengthen supply chains for critical minerals.On the sidelines, Jaishankar attended a Quad foreign ministers' meeting with Rubio and his Japanese and Australian counterparts. He also met Russian foreign minister Sergey Lavrov, with discussions covering the Ukraine conflict, the Gulf situation and multilateral issues.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: No more washing up: How Airbnb's new house rules have divided hosts and guests
articles.summary: Airbnb hosts must stop asking guests to wash-up or take out bins under rules coming into force in November.
articles.body:
When Lisa Clewes returned to her Welsh holiday let after a group of guests checked out, she was horrified by the mess.

Just days earlier, she had met the group in person and helped with their luggage.

But after a dinner party, the house was left "in a complete mess" with broken glasses, drinks cans on the floor, pans full of food on the table and fish guts left in the garden.

"It was really unbelievable. Had I had another booking the same day, I would have had to cancel or delay check-in," says Clewes.

She charges a cleaning fee that covers around 75% of the cost of a cleaner and asks guests to empty the fridge, put rubbish in the bins and load the dishwasher.

But Airbnb's new rules mean hosts can no longer ask guests to do jobs normally carried out by cleaners, including washing and putting away dishes, stripping beds and taking rubbish off site.

The updated guidelines, which apply to bookings made globally from 20 November, state that hosts can now set seven standard house rules and add other "reasonable" requests.

Clewes says it typically takes cleaners four hours to turn around her three-bedroom property. She fears guests leaving more mess could mean hiring extra cleaners and increasing costs – expenses that may ultimately be passed on to her guests.

The changes have come as a relief to guests like Jessica Newhook, who says she has been faced with lengthy checkout lists, often on top of hefty cleaning fees.

She booked an Airbnb in Florida for a family reunion of 11 guests and says they had to "leave the property move-in ready for the cleaners", despite paying a $250 (£187) cleaning fee.

Newhook says the host told them to wash and fold towels, clean the bedding and kitchen, and sweep and mop the floors. She was also warned by the host that their behaviour needed to improve or they could be told to leave, because they had left chairs blocking bins.

"We had rules about everything and it was not relaxing at all."

While Newhook likes the home comforts of staying in an Airbnb, she says the combination of relentless rules and rising cleaning fees has taken away much of its appeal.

"It is getting to the point where a hotel is cheaper and I know what to expect."

Krissi Foskett, 46, from Glasgow, runs a national cleaning company and regularly stays in Airbnb properties so "can see the issue from both sides".

During a recent stay in Stafford, she paid a £35 cleaning fee but was still asked to strip the beds, put on a wash, empty bins and carry rubbish down a long track to a recycling area.

"I don't particularly mind doing those things, but it did make me question what exactly I was paying the additional cleaning fee for," she says.

For Foskett, there is a difference between being a considerate guest – "putting your dirty dishes in the dishwasher" – and being "expected to prepare the property for the next guests".

Through her cleaning business, she has also seen the other extreme, with teams arriving to find broken furniture, vomit and pet urine.

While she sympathises with hosts facing tight turnarounds and rising cleaning costs, these should not be passed on to guests, she says.

"If you're running an Airbnb as a business, professional cleaning is a cost of doing business."

Anthony Marsh, who co-owns a cabin retreat in North Yorkshire with his husband, used to list five of their 12 properties on Airbnb, but says the new rules have prompted him to reduce this number to just two.

His concern with the changes is that "Airbnb has effectively given guests permission to come and leave properties a tip, and a host can't do anything about it".

He believes asking guests to wash their pots and put out the bins is hardly unreasonable and, with a small cleaning team and tight turnaround times, he worries extra mess could leave properties unready for the next arrivals.

"It's common sense and common decency," he says.

His company does not charge a cleaning fee, and Marsh says most guests are respectful. But fees are more common than not. Some 63.2% of Airbnb listings charge a cleaning fee, with an average cost of £55 according to data from AirROI .

Laura Lewis runs a directory that helps holiday-let owners market their properties and connect with potential guests.

Many of her clients also list on Airbnb and she says most are unhappy with the new rules, arguing that asking guests to wash up is a matter of basic respect.

"Some people say it's factored into the cleaning fee, but I wouldn't leave a holiday let with all the washing-up to do. It's not the right thing," she says.

The announcement has added to growing frustration among owners following increases in Airbnb's commission rates last year. Many are investing in their own websites and social media to attract direct bookings and avoid platform fees.

Lewis has taken the same approach with the three treehouses on her farm – most of her bookings are already direct and she now plans to remove her listings from Airbnb altogether.

Not all hosts are concerned about the changes, however. Matt Prosz, who hosts and manages other Airbnb properties full-time, believes the update will improve the guest experience without changing how most people behave.

Guests at his property in south-west London are asked only to lock up and return the keys. "People sometimes strip the beds or do things without me asking, and that's nice for my cleaners, but I don't expect it."

Prosz doubts the changes will lead to guests leaving properties in a worse state, pointing to Airbnb's mutual review system.

"If I put a big chore list, I wouldn't expect a five-star review and vice versa – if a guest leaves the place in a state, you're not going to give them a good review."

He believes the system encourages both sides to behave reasonably, and that most guests will continue to treat properties with respect.

"Airbnb is trying to cut out the silly stuff because it's not a good guest experience."

articles.title: A California real-estate CEO concealed his firm's financial troubles while collecting investments that left more than 20 people $2.2 million poorer; a federal judge has sentenced him to 18 months in prison
articles.summary: A real-estate business can face financial difficulties, but concealing those problems from investors can turn a struggling company into a fraud case.
articles.body: A real-estate business can face financial difficulties, but concealing those problems from investors can turn a struggling company into a fraud case. A California property developer who continued seeking investments while his company was heavily in debt and facing serious cash-flow problems has now been sentenced to federal prison. More than 20 investors lost over $2.2 million after trusting his representations about the business and its projects.In a press release issued on October 28, 2026, the US Attorney's Office for the Northern District of California announced that Sanjeev Acharya, former president and CEO of SiliconSage Builders, had been sentenced to 18 months in prison for wire fraud and money laundering. US District Judge Charles R. Breyer also ordered him to pay $2,253,219.84 in restitution to victims and serve two years of supervised release. Acharya is scheduled to begin his prison sentence on January 9, 2027.How the real-estate investment business operatedAcharya, 58, of San Jose, was the president and CEO of SiliconSage Builders and several related companies. The business operated as a vertically integrated development and construction company, supporting investments in large residential and mixed-use real-estate projects across the San Francisco Bay Area. As part of his role, Acharya personally approached investors and encouraged them to put money into the company's property developments. The investment model depended on attracting funds to support construction and other real-estate activities.However, the company's financial position had deteriorated significantly by 2020. According to the plea agreement, the business was struggling partly because of the COVID-19 pandemic and had accumulated substantial debt. It was also experiencing serious cash-flow shortages and needed fresh investments to remain operational. Rather than disclosing these difficulties to potential investors, Acharya continued seeking money for the business.How investors were misledThe fraudulent scheme began in March 2020 and continued until October 26, 2020. During this period, Acharya solicited investments without informing people about the company's actual financial condition. According to the US Attorney's Office, he knew SiliconSage was in serious financial trouble but concealed its debt and cash-flow problems while persuading investors to provide additional funds.The investors were therefore not given important information that could have influenced their decisions about whether to invest. They were unaware that the company was struggling financially and required new money to survive. More than 20 investors were deceived during the scheme. Together, they suffered losses exceeding $2.2 million. The case highlights how financial difficulties within a property development business can affect people who invest their savings based on the expectation that their money will support viable projects.CEO pleaded guilty to wire fraud and a financial offenceAcharya was charged on September 5, 2025, in connection with the investment fraud. Rather than proceeding to trial, he pleaded guilty on January 6, 2026, to wire fraud and engaging in a monetary transaction involving property derived from fraud. Wire fraud is a federal offence involving the use of electronic communications or other forms of interstate communication to carry out a fraudulent scheme. The money laundering-related offence in his case concerned conducting a financial transaction with money obtained through unlawful activity.The investigation was conducted by the Internal Revenue Service Criminal Investigation (IRS-CI), which examined the financial transactions and the movement of money connected with the scheme. US Attorney Craig H. Missakian said financial difficulties could never justify deceiving investors. He added that the prison sentence held Acharya accountable and demonstrated that people who exploit investors for financial gain could face serious consequences. John Abram, acting special agent in charge of the IRS-CI San Francisco Field Office, also highlighted the impact of financial fraud on individuals and families. He said the losses could put retirement plans, educational opportunities and financial security at risk.Court orders more than $2.25 million in restitutionUS District Judge Charles R. Breyer sentenced Acharya to 18 months in federal prison. In addition to the prison term, the judge imposed two years of supervised release and ordered him to pay $2,253,219.84 in restitution to the victims. Restitution is intended to compensate people who suffered financial losses because of a criminal offence. In this case, the amount ordered by the court reflects the financial harm caused to investors through the fraudulent scheme. Acharya is scheduled to report to prison on January 9, 2027.Assistant US Attorney Christiaan Highsmith prosecuted the case, with assistance from Janice Pagsanjan, Mimi Lam and Kevin Costello. The prosecution followed the investigation conducted by IRS-CI. The case serves as a reminder that property investment companies must be transparent about their financial condition when raising money. Even when a business is attempting to survive difficult market conditions, withholding important financial information from investors can carry serious criminal consequences.You use AI every day. articles.title: How the downfall of Serbia's Vučiċ mirrored that of Hungary's Orbán
articles.summary: Defeat for Serbia's Aleksandar Vučiċ in last weekend's vote was a carbon copy of Viktor Orbán's fall in Hungary.
articles.body:
When they met in northern Serbia last November, Serbian President Aleksandar Vučiċ and Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orbán could hardly have guessed they would both be out of power within a year.

Both were ousted by popular movements - Orbán fell first, in April, defeated by Péter Magyar's Tisza party. Then last Sunday a student movement less than two years old won Serbia's parliamentary elections by a landslide.

The Tisza party in Hungary and the Student List in Serbia look very different - Tisza is centred on the personality and energy of its leader, while the students in Serbia insist they have no leadership.

But the huge turnout - 79% in Hungary and 69% in Serbia, was driven by tech-savvy young people in both countries. They used AI tools to crunch numbers, identify threats to the vote, and mobilise tens of thousands of election monitors to prevent intimidation and electoral fraud by the governing parties.

Mobilisation of voters, and the role of election monitors, played a big role in the opposition victory in both countries.

Last weekend, the DE civic action group in Hungary sent 70 election monitors to Serbia, to work with students' movement representatives, visiting polling stations in the northern Serbian province of Vojvodina.

During the summer, even before the election was called, they held workshops to share their experience and methods from the Hungarian election with the Serbian students.

A key technique was to identify "infected" polling districts in advance - places where the surprisingly high number of votes for the governing party at previous elections suggested that voter intimidation or "chain voting" techniques were used.

"From around 16:00 on election day, we noticed groups of masked hooligans - Vučiċ supporters - gathering near voting stations," Péter Klemm, a student activist from Subotica, told the BBC. "So we sent mobile teams, and started filming everything."

Combined with the "stationary" monitors already in place, 20 to 30 volunteers at each threatened polling station acted as a strong deterrent, he believes, and prevented intimidation or fraud.

Orbán in Hungary, Vučiċ in Serbia, both looked invincible. Both were powerful leaders, in office for 16 and 14 years, who had taken over state institutions and established business empires overlapping the two countries.

Orban chose cheese, Vučiċ meat, when they sat down to a quick lunch of traditional burek pastries at a small, popular town centre bakery in Subotica almost a year ago.

They continued to a local winery, to talk about oil and other business deals - the planned Hungarian purchase of Serbia's Nis oil refinery. The two nationalist leaders found much in common, in business and politics, not least their friendship with Vladimir Putin in Russia and Chinese President Xi Jinping, and their strong support for Milorad Dodik, the separatist leader of the Bosnian Serbs.

A high-speed railway between Belgrade and Budapest is being built with Chinese finance and know-how.

The parallels between the fall from power of the two men are extraordinary. Aleksandar Vučiċ admitted defeat at exactly 21:30 on Sunday evening, just as Viktor Orbán did on 12 April. Few observers expected either leader to concede peacefully.

There has been speculation this week that Vučiċ spoke to Orbán twice on Sunday night to ask his advice - once before he conceded, and again at 23:15. And that Orbán convinced his Serbian ally not to use force.

Vučiċ denies that he spoke to Orbán before he made his announcement, but acknowledges the later conversation. Viktor Orbán, contacted by the BBC, declined to comment.

An hour before polls closed in Serbia, masked and hooded vigilantes took up position in central Belgrade. During voting, similar groups were photographed at many polling stations, and blocked by election monitors.

There is another strange numerical similarity. The Student List will have 140 seats in the 250-seat Serbian parliament, the same number Péter Magyar's Tisza party won in the 199-seat Hungarian parliament.

Magyar was the only European leader to ring the students directly to congratulate them that evening - and probably the only one who had their number.

"It is always good to hear that the story of Tisza could provide an inspiration for other nations," the Hungarian prime minister told the BBC.

"The result of the Hungarian election clearly showed us that what we are doing here is right," the head of the Student List, Ilija Srdanoviċ, said on the eve of the vote.

Srdanoviċ was one of those Péter Magyar spoke to that Sunday evening.

Orbán, 63, and Vučiċ, 56, may now both face prosecution for corruption and abuse of power.

The judicial machinery in both countries is similar. Serbia's special prosecution service for organised crime, JTOK, and Hungary's brand new special prosecutors, known as NVVH, have similar powers. They could prove useful to each other.

Hungarian companies close to Orbán were also involved in the Novi Sad railway station construction project. The collapse of the station's canopy on 1 November 2024 - blamed on corruption, as well as negligence - killed 16 people, and acted as the catalyst for the Serbian student movement.

"There was a perception in Europe that the longer the Orbán and Vučiċ regimes stayed in office, the stronger they got," Áron Timar, founder of the DE civic action group in Hungary told the BBC.

"In fact they got weaker. And once society found its voice and rose up, there was no way of stopping it."

articles.title: FBI links record $6.3 billion Binance crypto theft to North Korea
articles.summary: Investing.com -- The FBI has accused North Korea of orchestrating the $6.3 billion cryptocurrency hack targeting Binance, identifying a state-linked hacking...
articles.body:
Investing.com -- The FBI has accused North Korea of orchestrating the $6.3 billion cryptocurrency hack targeting Binance, identifying a state-linked hacking group responsible for previous major crypto thefts as the perpetrators.

The agency said Saturday that the North Korean hacking unit known as TraderTraitor was responsible for the attack, which ranks as the largest cryptocurrency theft on record.

The FBI, working alongside the U.S. Secret Service and the Internal Revenue Service's criminal investigation division, has been tracking movements of the stolen digital assets.

Investigators observed the hackers converting stolen cryptocurrencies primarily into Ethereum, with further laundering expected through decentralized finance platforms and instant cryptocurrency swap services.

The findings mark the first formal attribution of the Binance attack to North Korea following earlier speculation about the country's involvement.

President Donald Trump said Friday that U.S. authorities were investigating whether North Korean hackers were behind the theft.

Binance, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange, separately announced Saturday that it had covered approximately 90% of the $6.3 billion stolen in the attack.

The exchange expects to restore customer withdrawals by Sunday as it works to complete recovery efforts.

Binance reiterated that it would absorb the entire financial impact of the breach, promising that customers would not suffer losses from the incident.

The unprecedented theft has raised fresh concerns about security across the cryptocurrency industry as digital asset platforms seek broader institutional and retail adoption.

TraderTraitor has previously been linked to several high-profile cryptocurrency attacks, including the $1.5 billion theft from Bybit in 2025.

North Korean hackers have also been accused of carrying out a separate cryptocurrency theft worth approximately $620 million in 2022.

The FBI's attribution comes amid renewed discussion of potential diplomatic engagement between Washington and Pyongyang.

Trump has recently suggested another meeting with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un could take place this year, although he later expressed uncertainty about whether either side was seeking talks.

articles.title: Newspaper headlines: 'PM lets down the King' and 'Kenny's secret night at Maya's'
articles.summary: Many of Sunday's front pages look at what Andy Burnham's comments on an apology for slavery mean for the King.
articles.body:
Warning: Sunday's paper review contains spoilers for The Celebrity Traitors.

The Sunday Times leads with Rachel Reeves' comments on the UK rejoining the EU - noting that, in her article, the former chancellor does not offer any thoughts on a timeline, or whether a fresh referendum would be needed. The chief minister of Gibraltar is much more forthcoming: Fabian Picardo tells the Sunday Mirror he is looking forward to seeing the issue go before the British people once again, in a "very clear manifesto commitment", or a fresh public vote.

In the Sunday Telegraph, Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch accuses the government of making unfunded spending promises that will need to be paid for through tax rises. She says proposals including setting up a National Care Service have left a "colossal" black hole in the public finances after the budget. The Treasury tells the paper the budget met fiscal rules and set borrowing on a downward path.

"An ill-timed intervention that's triggered a fresh call for billions" is h ow the Mail on Sunday sees Andy Burnham's suggestion that the UK could apologise for its role in the transatlantic slave trade. An editorial in The Sunday Express accuses the prime minister of having made life harder for King Charles III during his Caribbean tour and suggests he stop "shooting from the hip" to avoid sowing international chaos. The last thing this country needs, says the Sun on Sunday , is what the paper calls a new chorus of financial demands from governments, lawyers and bleeding-heart campaigners.

The Sunday Times reports on claims that an AI programme ignored the evidence given to a landmark maternity review by women who say they were harmed by a drive for births with no medical intervention. The Amos review concluded in June that what is known as "normal birth ideology" was not widespread in maternity care in England. But the paper says there were many devastating accounts among the more than 10,000 responses which, the Times has learned, were fed into Microsoft Copilot, with NHS staff asking it to "identity themes and produce summaries". Former Health Secretary Sir Jeremy Hunt tells the paper the allegations are deeply troubling. Baroness Amos did not respond to a request for comment.

The lead story for the Sunday Mirror is an investigation into cosmetics firms up-selling surgery abroad. A surgeon is said to have tried to "flog a Brazilian buttlift" to an undercover reporter. The Mirror's editorial advises that world-class surgery comes with a world-class price and any offer of cheaper rates should be handled with care.

There is no let-up in the pressure on the Manchester United manager Michael Carrick on the back pages after his team's loss to Chelsea. The Telegraph says it was a "Halloween Horror" that puts the club on its worst run of results since 1988. For the Star, Carrick's spell at the club is now surely "deader than disco".

articles.title: Meet Nicolina Pappas, 13, the Illinois teenager whose campaign against single-use plastic reached 14 US cities, secured 14 official proclamations and raised over $15,000 for conservation
articles.summary: Nicolina Pappas, the 13-year-old single-use plastic campaigner from Rock Island, Illinois, is fighting plastic pollution through her company, Nicolina’s
articles.body: Nicolina Pappas, the 13-year-old single-use plastic campaigner from Rock Island, Illinois, is fighting plastic pollution through her company, Nicolina’s Turtle Co., and her Skip the Plastic Campaign. The campaign has reached 14 cities in the United States and secured 14 official proclamations, while the company has raised more than $15,000 for conservation. Her efforts earned second place, alongside winners from Kenya and India, in the age group for children aged eight to 13 at the 2025 International Young Eco-Hero Awards. Those awards recognise young people aged eight to 16 who take practical action against climate change, pollution and wildlife loss.How Nicolina Pappas turned her concern for sea turtles into handmade straw pouches and a movementNicolina has been an environmental advocate since she was eight years old. Her compassion for sea turtles, which are hurt by plastic straws, led her to design and sew small pouches that she sold alongside metal straws. That modest idea evolved into a movement that now influences policy at local and state level.Five years of fundraising and public speaking have carried her small business to non-profit statusMoney raised over the past five years goes through local organisations to pay for river cleanups, conservation camp scholarships and classroom outreach. Nicolina also teaches in person, having spoken to roughly 3,500 students and adults at summits, conferences, classrooms and city councils. Her company recently achieved non-profit status, extending its reach and impact.A setback over her straw ban led Nicolina to a just-ask approach that won support for less plasticJoel Vanderbush, Curator of Conservation and Education at Niabi Zoo and Nicolina’s mentor, told Action For Nature he has never met a child her age so driven and motivated to change the environment. He explained that her first proposal to her city council, a ban on plastic straws, faced setbacks, so she pivoted to a “just ask” policy, which brought a mayoral proclamation.Her most recent project, the Skip the Plastic Campaign, follows the same principle. It asks restaurants to provide plastic items only on request and invites customers to politely decline them. There is no mandate, a choice rooted in Nicolina’s understanding of environmental justice and the financial burden that bans can place on underserved communities.From city councils to state lawmakers, her resolutions made April 1 Skip the Plastic Day in IllinoisThe campaign’s proclamations cover more than 250,000 residents across Illinois and Iowa, yet Nicolina did not stop at the city level. She authored state resolutions that made April 1 Skip the Plastic Day across Illinois, and she testified before both the state House and the Senate.Nicolina told Action For Nature, the San Francisco non-profit behind the awards, that she has learned she can achieve much more by recruiting partners and asking for advice than by doing everything on her own. She now wants to take the Skip the Plastic Campaign to other states and eventually to the federal level, and she hopes to become a marine biologist or a lawyer.You use AI every day. articles.title: NYC woman critically injured after being stabbed multiple times while jogging along Brooklyn waterfront
articles.summary: A 28-year-old woman was stabbed in the neck while jogging along Brooklyn's Shore Parkway in New York City, and NYPD has no suspect identified.
articles.body: A 28-year-old woman was critically injured after being stabbed multiple times in the neck while jogging along a Brooklyn waterfront path Friday night, New York City police confirmed to Fox News Digital. The attack occurred around 8 p.m. near Shore Parkway and Bay 17th Street in Brooklyn's Bath Beach neighborhood, according to the New York Police Department. Police said the woman was jogging eastbound along the Shore Parkway Greenway when she suffered multiple stab wounds to the neck. Emergency medical personnel transported her to NYU Langone Hospital-Brooklyn in critical condition. MAN DEAD, ANOTHER CRITICAL AFTER DOUBLE STABBING AT BROOKLYN PARK AS POLICE DETAIN PERSON OF INTEREST: NYPD An NYPD spokesperson confirmed to Fox News Digital on Saturday that the woman remained alive. Police have not released her identity, and investigators have not identified a suspect, the spokesperson said. The New York Post reported that the woman had been training for Sunday's New York City Marathon, citing police sources. In a statement to Fox News Digital, New York Road Runners (NYRR), which organizes the marathon, expressed sympathy for the victim and her family. GEORGIA JOGGER RUNS FOR HER LIFE AFTER STRANGER ALLEGEDLY TRIES TO MOW HER DOWN 3 TIMES "We were sad to hear of this horrible attack—our hearts are with her family and the running community," the organization said. NYRR also said its records show the woman had previously participated in its races but could not confirm whether she planned to run in Sunday's marathon. It was not immediately clear what led up to the attack or whether the victim knew her attacker. The attack occurred along a section of the waterfront path overlooking Gravesend Bay, with views of Staten Island and the Verrazzano-Narrows Bridge, the Post reported. Police are asking the public for help as the investigation continues. articles.title: Second night of drone disruption at Jersey Airport
articles.summary: Jersey Airport said it was "experiencing disruption.... affecting inbound flights as a result of further drone activity".
articles.body:
People at Jersey Airport have said they are frustrated and angry that "unauthorised drone" activity caused more flight cancellations for a second night in a row.

At 20:05 on Saturday Jersey Airport said it was "experiencing disruption.... affecting inbound flights as a result of further drone activity in the vicinity of the airfield".

States of Jersey Police are investigating the incidents and officers have appealed to anyone with information about who is responsible to come forward.

Insp Rob McCallum said it was believed "two or three" drones had entered the restricted airspace, but they were not thought to be linked to terrorism.

The Chief Minister of Jersey, Senator Lyndon Farnham, said operating a drone close to an airport was "not a prank or a harmless hobby".

"To those responsible, the message is clear: if you are identified, you should expect to face the full consequences of the law," he added.

Pacific Basirwe was waiting for his wife and young son to fly in from London Heathrow when he heard the news.

He said: "It's annoying, this should be regulated, and the people doing those things should be prosecuted.

"It's been two days in a row now… If there is no further action, they will keep doing it, which is not good."

Richard De La Haye has been a taxi driver for more than 40 years and believes the drone activity is affecting business for drivers like him.

He said: "It's a bit of a nightmare because we're sitting here for a couple of hours really not knowing what's going to happen."

De La Haye added: "If we pull away and the flights come in then people will be stranded waiting for taxis but if they don't come in we're sat here for two hours waiting for passengers.

"It's getting silly and I don't know the answer, but it really needs to be resolved, quite honestly."

articles.summary: Iran's senior security official Mohsen Rezaei on Saturday claimed that the United States had significantly softened its approach towards Tehran in a
articles.body: Iran's senior security official Mohsen Rezaei on Saturday claimed that the United States had significantly softened its approach towards Tehran in a letter sent by Vice President JD Vance, describing the shift in tone as a sign of Iran's victory.His remarks mark the first public response from an Iranian official to Washington's diplomatic outreach, even as US President Donald Trump continues to claim that Tehran is keen to negotiate.“Their tone has shifted completely, which is a good sign that shows that our people have secured their victory,” Rezaei told Iranian state broadcaster IRIB, as quoted by ANI.The letter, addressed to Rezaei, secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, was delivered through Qatari mediators on Sunday. According to The New York Times, the proposal suggests holding direct negotiations under Vance's leadership, with Iran's nuclear programme included in the discussions from the outset.However, The Wall Street Journal, citing a source familiar with the matter, reported that the communication laid out a broad "framework for negotiations" rather than specific conditions for a peace agreement. The letter was reportedly sent on Trump's instructions.Earlier, Iranian foreign minister Abbas Araghchi told Al Jazeera on Saturday that Tehran had examined the communication and viewed Washington's outreach as a "positive step" towards dialogue. He also said one of his aides had travelled to Doha for consultations with mediators.Citing sources, Al Jazeera reported that a meeting between the two sides could take place within a week, with Doha and Istanbul being considered as possible venues.Iran warns US, Israel against further attacksAmid the diplomatic overtures, Iranian supreme leader Mojtaba Khamenei warned that the country's armed forces would respond to any miscalculation by the US or Israel with retaliation that would be “geographically unrestricted”.“If the enemies once again launch military or terrorist attacks, it is the armed forces of the Islamic republic and the Iranian nation that will determine the time and conditions for their end,” Khamenei said.Meanwhile, Trump reiterated his claim that Tehran was keen to negotiate during remarks at the White House on Friday."There are talks, they want to talk, they keep talking," the US president said, adding, "We have time, frankly."Trump also claimed that Iran was "in a lot of trouble" and expressed confidence that the ongoing conflict would end “very soon”.You use AI every day. articles.title: Reeves says UK's future should be inside the EU
articles.summary: In her first major intervention since leaving the Treasury, Rachel Reeves says Brexit has made the UK "poorer, weaker and less secure".
articles.body:
Former Chancellor Rachel Reeves has argued the UK's future should be inside the EU, and that Brexit has made the country "poorer, weaker and less secure".

In her first major intervention since leaving the Treasury, Reeves said she welcomed debate around the UK's relationship with Europe.

At the last election, Labour's manifesto said a Labour government would stay outside the EU and make Brexit work.

But Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said there needs to be an honest discussion about what the future relationship looks like.

The Conservatives have said there is no desire to rerun the Brexit debate and Reform UK's Nigel Farage has said there is no mandate to pursue closer EU ties.

Labour's 2024 election manifesto ruled out a return of free movement, single market membership or a customs union.

Burnham has said that any changes would require a mandate at a general election, which is next due by 2029.

In the Sunday Times , Reeves wrote: "No-one in the Treasury ever doubted where my instincts were. I do believe Britain's future lies in the European Union."

She said supporters of rejoining the EU had to "make the argument, demonstrate tangible benefits and to get the next steps right".

Reeves added that at the forthcoming UK-EU summit, she hoped for confirmation of the youth mobility scheme she has been pushing for since she was in office.

She also said she was hoping for "progress towards entry" into the Security Action for Europe (SAFE) scheme.

Announced last March, SAFE is part of an EU-wide effort to rearm after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

A defence pact agreed with the EU last May paved the way for UK-based defence companies to be part of projects funded by SAFE.

In her piece for the Sunday Times, Reeves also sought to defend her record in office.

She wrote about the need for governments to be "braver" in building big infrastructure projects and "clear eyed" about the risks and benefits AI would drive in advanced economies.

articles.title: Epstein letter row: Judge rejects Trump's $10 billion defamation suit against WSJ
articles.summary: A federal judge in the United States on Saturday dismissed president Donald Trump’s $10 billion defamation lawsuit against The Wall Street Journal for the
articles.body: A federal judge in the United States on Saturday dismissed president Donald Trump’s $10 billion defamation lawsuit against The Wall Street Journal for the second time this year. The court ruled that Trump had failed to establish that the newspaper acted with “actual malice” in its reporting on an alleged birthday letter bearing his name and linked to convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.US district Judge Darrin P Gayles, sitting in Miami, dismissed the lawsuit with prejudice, meaning Trump cannot refile the same case. Describing the president’s arguments as “grasping at straws”, the judge said the amended complaint failed to meet the legal threshold for establishing defamation.According to the Associated Press (AP), this is the second time Gayles has dismissed Trump's lawsuit this year. The judge first threw out the case in April, ruling that Trump had failed to sufficiently argue that the newspaper published the report with actual malice. However, Gayles allowed the president to file an amended complaint, which was submitted in May. The revised lawsuit has now also been dismissed.“The Amended Complaint falls short of pleading actual malice,” Gayles wrote.“Indeed, the allegations regarding malice are conclusory, vague, sometimes inconsistent with the Article, and often irrelevant to whether Defendants knew or should have known that the statements in the Article were purportedly false,” he added.The lawsuit arose from a Wall Street Journal report published last year about a sexually suggestive letter and drawing that the newspaper said bore Trump's name. The material was reportedly included in an album compiled for Epstein's 50th birthday in 2003.According to the newspaper, the letter was collected by British socialite Ghislaine Maxwell. It contained text framed by the outline of what appeared to be a hand-drawn naked woman and ended with the words: “Happy Birthday -- and may every day be another wonderful secret.”Trump denied writing the letter and described the report as “false, malicious, and defamatory”.His lawsuit accused Dow Jones, the newspaper's parent company, Rupert Murdoch and other defendants of having “knowingly and recklessly” published “numerous false, defamatory, and disparaging statements”. It also alleged “overwhelming financial and reputational harm” and sought $10 billion in damages.Gayles rejected the argument that the newspaper should have withheld its report following Trump's denial.“Rather, it informed readers that President Trump decried the Letter as a fake and denied writing it,” the judge wrote.In his ruling, Gayles cited the US Supreme Court's 1964 judgment in New York Times Co. v. Sullivan, which requires public figures to establish that a publication knowingly made false statements or acted with reckless disregard for the truth.The dismissal comes amid Trump's wider legal confrontations with media organisations, including disputes involving the BBC and The Associated Press. CNN, MS NOW and Politico have also pursued legal action over their White House access.Trump's legal team could challenge the latest ruling through an appeal.You use AI every day. articles.title: Ukrainian evacuees from Russian-occupied Oleshky reunite with family
articles.summary: Starved and exhausted residents of Oleshky arrive in Ukraine after months of isolation, but some stay behind.
articles.body:
Starved and exhausted residents of the Russian-occupied Ukrainian town of Oleshky have crossed into Ukraine in a major evacuation operation of civilians, under the first humanitarian truce of its kind in more than four years of Moscow’s war.

The six-day ceasefire covering the town was reached with mediation efforts by US First Lady Melania Trump and help from Pope Leo XIV. It is the longest local pause in fighting since Russia’s full-scale invasion of its neighbour in 2022.

“Ukrainian citizens from Oleshky have crossed the Ukrainian border in the Chernihiv region. All of them will receive the assistance they need,” Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy wrote on X, thanking the United States and the first lady for mediating.

“Further steps toward de-escalation and real progress toward peace are also needed,” he added.

Evacuees wrapped in blue and yellow Ukrainian flags stepped off buses at the Ukrainian-Belarusian border and reunited with family members.

Ukrainian officials met the evacuees with posters reading “You’re not alone” and “We embrace with our hearts”, while residents from nearby villages lined the highway waving flags and flashlights to greet them.

Supply routes to Oleshky had been disrupted by fighting and drones. According to some residents, food deliveries were stopped in May, pushing hundreds of people into starvation.

One evacuee, an elderly man in a wheelchair, told the Reuters news agency that he had lost 20kg (44lbs) over the past year, becoming so weak he required hospital treatment.

Another evacuee, Svitlana Yermakova, told Reuters they had to eat grass to survive.

“We chopped grass and squash… just to hold on,” she said, adding that she risked riding by bicycle through minefields to a nearby village to get food for herself and her dog.

To reach Ukrainian-held territory, Oleshky residents had to take a complicated route to leave the devastated town just a few kilometres from the front line.

They first crossed Crimea by bus to the Russian town of Anapa before flying to Belarus, from where they crossed into Ukraine.

Ambulances lined the street, and several large military tents were erected, where hot meals, tea and medical aid were provided.

Russian and Ukrainian officials say the ceasefire in Oleshky has held since Tuesday, allowing them to de-mine the roads and bring food, medicines and other supplies into the town again.

The truce is due to end on Sunday evening.

Some residents have decided to remain in Oleshky, despite the ongoing lack of gas, electricity and running water.

Russian Human Rights Commissioner Yana Lantratova said living conditions in the occupied Oleshky remained difficult, pledging she would continue to work with her Ukrainian counterpart, Dmytro Lubinets, to help those who stayed.

“The mission has come to an end,” she said on Telegram. “We have agreed to carry out regular humanitarian missions, which is a very important step.”

Oleshky had a pre-war population of about 24,000, which plunged to an estimated 1,700 before the evacuation.

Ukrainian officials have not said exactly how many residents were evacuated or how many remained.

Despite the ceasefire in Oleshky, fighting rages on in other parts of the front, with Russia and Ukraine keeping up drone attacks against each other.

articles.title: Halloween, protests and chaos -  why is Gen Z taking to the streets across Germany
articles.summary: Thousands of young people took to the streets across Germany on Saturday to protest against rising living costs, cuts in education spending and plans to
articles.body: Thousands of young people took to the streets across Germany on Saturday to protest against rising living costs, cuts in education spending and plans to strengthen the country's military, but demonstrations in several cities turned violent in the evening, with rioters looting shops and clashing with police.The protests, organised by the youth campaign group "GenZ regelt!" (Gen Z takes charge), were held in 34 cities, including Berlin, Frankfurt and Munich. The movement drew inspiration from youth-led demonstrations in other European countries, particularly France and Italy, where young people have been demanding greater attention to their concerns.While the demonstrations remained largely peaceful during the day, violence broke out in major cities including Frankfurt, Berlin, Cologne and Hamburg as some groups refused to disperse.According to AFP, masked rioters looted shops in Frankfurt, while police used water cannons and pepper spray against demonstrators who threw stones, fireworks and petrol bombs at security personnel and emergency workers.Police described the situation in Frankfurt as involving "violent riots" and said several shops had their windows smashed. Molotov cocktails were also thrown at emergency personnel, according to a police statement cited by AFP.A gun store was among the establishments targeted, with its windows smashed. Police arrested a suspect and seized two weapons. A trainer shop and a perfume store were also reportedly looted, according to German daily Bild.A large section of Frankfurt's main shopping street was closed as police attempted to bring the situation under control. Police vans and riot officers prevented people from entering the area, while a helicopter hovered overhead.At least one police officer was injured in Frankfurt and received medical treatment. Police also reported injuries to officers in other cities.Police blame extremist groups for violenceAuthorities said the protests had been infiltrated by extremist groups, raising concerns about the possibility of violence spreading during demonstrations.Roman Poseck, interior minister of the German state of Hesse, said around 100 identified left-wing extremists had joined the protest in Frankfurt."It is shameful how this event here in Frankfurt has ended," Poseck said.Police also deployed water cannons in Hamburg and Cologne after demonstrators allegedly targeted emergency service personnel with fireworks, stones and bottles.In Berlin, a separate evening protest, which was not organised by the GenZ regelt! movement, saw demonstrators throw eggs and bottles at police. A police officer in Bonn also suffered minor injuries during a confrontation with a group.According to Reuters, Germany's federal interior ministry had warned ahead of the demonstrations that parts of the country's far-left extremist scene and groups linked to foreign extremist movements were trying to mobilise support.Hesse's interior minister had also cautioned against the possibility of violence similar to the unrest witnessed in France."We all have those images from France in our minds - looting, burning houses, burning police vehicles, and attacks on police officers," Poseck told Reuters."France must not be held up as a model in this regard."Some businesses in German cities had boarded up their windows and planned to close early ahead of the demonstrations. Concerns were particularly high along Berlin's luxury Kurfuerstendamm shopping boulevard.The GenZ regelt! movement, however, distanced itself from violence and said extremist groups had no place in its demonstrations."Extremist groups, anti-constitutional symbols, racism and hate speech have no place with us - no matter from which side," the group said.What are Germany's Gen Z protesters demanding?The demonstrations were driven by concerns over the rising cost of living, the condition of schools and universities, government spending cuts and increased military expenditure.The movement also opposes compulsory military service and has called for greater investment in education and public services.Young people in Germany have expressed concerns about the government's plans to increase troop numbers through a new voluntary military service model, fearing that it could eventually lead to the return of compulsory conscription.The protests come at a time when Europe's largest economy is struggling to revive growth and facing increasing pressure on its pension system and public services.Germany is also dealing with demographic challenges as large sections of the baby boomer generation approach retirement, reducing the size of its working-age population and putting additional pressure on younger generations.For many protesters, the issue is not limited to military policy or education spending but also concerns the government's priorities and the financial burden being placed on young people."The government has offered no response to our concerns other than to continue making cuts and piling further burdens upon us," Steve, an 18-year-old scheduled to address a rally in Munich, told Reuters.Addressing Chancellor Friedrich Merz, he said the protesters would continue exercising their right to assemble until their concerns were addressed.In Berlin, Technical University student Sean Baker told Reuters that the poor condition of university buildings was among the reasons he planned to join the demonstration."When you go inside and enter the rooms, it looks like an abandoned building," he said. "Yet this is where we're expected to study on a regular basis."Turnout falls short of organisers' expectationsThe demonstrations were planned across 34 German cities, with organisers initially expecting around 182,000 participants.However, official figures available on Saturday afternoon indicated that turnout was significantly lower than anticipated.Police in Frankfurt, Munich and Berlin reported around 6,000 participants, compared with approximately 36,000 recorded on the organisers' website, Reuters reported.The movement's organisers later said around 120,000 people had participated nationwide, below their initial estimate of about 180,000, AFP reported.The demonstrations also coincided with Halloween celebrations, with some participants dressed in costumes ranging from dinosaurs to Batman. Protesters carried placards with slogans such as "Time for resistance" and "Merz must go", targeting the policies of the conservative chancellor.In Berlin, a 20-year-old student identified only as Milla told AFP that she wanted to show solidarity with similar demonstrations taking place across Europe."I've been waiting for a long time for something to finally really happen, and for people to tackle this with a bit more force. I believe that today here is the first step," she said.Questions over who is leading the movementDespite its youth-focused agenda, questions have emerged over whether GenZ regelt! is genuinely a student-led movement, given the involvement of a broad mix of political and civil society groups.Germany's national school student umbrella organisation, BSK, has distanced itself from the campaign and announced plans to organise a separate day of protests on November 20."We are distancing ourselves from 'GenZ regelt' but not from the students themselves, who have legitimate concerns," BSK Secretary-General Amy Kirchhoff said on Thursday, according to Reuters.The distinction highlights a wider debate over who represents Germany's younger generation and how their concerns should be raised.The protests are part of a wider wave of Gen Z-led demonstrations across Europe this year. In Serbia, student-led activism played a role in challenging the country's political leadership, while demonstrations in France have witnessed clashes, looting and widespread unrest.The developments have prompted German authorities to remain cautious about the possibility of similar violence spreading to the country.You use AI every day. articles.title: In 1961, a retired Georgia waiter began filling his home and yard with handmade figures; decades later became part of the Smithsonian’s efforts to preserve American history
articles.summary: In 1961, Dilmus Hall stepped away from his working life in Athens, Georgia, and began spending more time on the creations that had interested him since
articles.body: In 1961, Dilmus Hall stepped away from his working life in Athens, Georgia, and began spending more time on the creations that had interested him since childhood. Concrete, wood and whatever else he could find became materials for figures that gradually filled the yard and walls of his modest home. Some depicted religious scenes, while others reflected his understanding of good and evil, with symbols he believed could protect the household. Hall had no children of his own, but he often spoke of his sculptures as the children he continued to make. Years later, his work became part of a wider effort to preserve the artistic traditions of African American communities in the American South.How farming, coal mines and army service shaped Hall’s early yearHall grew up in a farming and blacksmithing family near Athens, where artistic interests competed with the practical demands of rural life. As a boy, he fashioned small animals from clay and a mixture made with flour and sweet gum. His mother welcomed these early efforts, though his father expected him to concentrate on farm work, including picking cotton.Art was not his livelihood for most of his early adulthood. Hall left the family farm and worked in a coal mine before joining a road gang. In 1917, he enlisted in the US Army Medical Corps and served in Europe as a stretcher-bearer. The experience exposed him to European art, which later influenced some of his sculptures.After returning to Georgia, Hall took a succession of jobs. He worked as a hotel bell captain and waiter, served as a busboy at a sorority house at the University of Georgia, and made concrete blocks for a construction company.Hall retired in 1961. By then, he had married Zaydie, whom he remembered affectionately. The couple were unable to have children, a fact Hall later addressed through his own particular understanding of his artistic work.Concrete figures began to change the look of his homeDuring the 1950s, Hall had already started making groups of figures from concrete laid over frameworks of wire and wood. He arranged them in the front yard of his small cinderblock house, turning the space into a setting for scenes drawn from religious belief and everyday conduct.Retirement gave him more time to continue this work. Rather than treating the house as separate from his art, Hall incorporated his creations into its surroundings. The walls, windows, roofline and yard all became places for painted shapes, sculpted objects and handmade decorations.Concrete provided a durable substance for figures and ornaments, while wood, putty, fabric and other found objects allowed him to create different forms. The results were not limited to conventional sculptures intended to stand alone. Hall's work developed across the property, with individual objects contributing to a larger arrangement.One of the best-known examples is The Devil and the Drunk Man, a tableau from the 1950s. It depicts two men affected by alcohol while a threatening devil looms over them. Hall explained the scene through his belief that Satan could influence people's behaviour and draw them towards wrongdoing. The sculpture gave physical form to that understanding of temptation and its consequences.Blue hands, diamonds and symbols of protectionHall's art also extended into the decoration of the house itself. Blue, yellow and red appeared across different surfaces, alongside crosses, diamonds, circles and sun shapes. Some of these motifs were positioned around windows, on the walls or beneath the roofline.A cement ball in the yard, dated 1962, carried two blue hands. The object has been associated with the African American tradition of the mojo or hand, a charm connected with protection and spiritual power. Hall also placed protective objects made from roots along the eaves of his porch. These early constructions were understood in relation to traditions in which particular objects were believed to guard against harmful forces.The blue decorations around his windows were part of a broader Southern and Caribbean tradition in which the colour was associated with protection. Hall used wooden plaques bearing white diamonds, while yellow cement diamonds marked the corners of his house. A rising sun appeared on the gable, with a sun and moon bearing smiling faces on the wall below.According to the account published by Souls Grown Deep, he used crosses and diamonds without knowing their connections to Central African symbolism. He nevertheless believed the forms had protective power.His work has been discussed in the context of African American conjuring culture, a set of spiritual practices shaped by African traditions and Christianity. In this context, objects may carry meanings beyond their physical appearance. They can serve as protective devices, preserve stories or express a person's place within a community.Religious scenes and drawings continued into later lifeHall's interest in religious subjects took several forms. In addition to his concrete figures, he made wooden crucifixions using materials such as putty and scraps of cloth. Some depicted Jesus on the cross alongside the two thieves, with details that gave the scenes a distinctly personal character.One crucifixion, made from wood and painted blue, used a relatively simple design. Other works included a Roman soldier and a spear, with Hall explaining the meaning of a splinter held in Jesus's mouth as an image of death being crushed between his teeth. The descriptions reveal how he interpreted the scenes through his own words rather than relying only on familiar religious imagery.He also painted a horse in the 1940s, which he identified as his first painting. Diamonds appeared above and below the animal. The work brought together his interest in painting and the recurring shapes that appeared elsewhere around his home.In later years, Hall produced hundreds of drawings using coloured pencils and crayons. Many had a cartoon-like appearance, while others returned to religious subjects. His work continued to move between sculpture, painting and drawing, without being confined to a single material or format.How Hall's work became part of a wider artistic historyHall's creations are now documented by Souls Grown Deep, an organisation devoted to preserving and presenting the work of African American artists from the American South. Its profile of Hall, written by Maude Southwell Wahlman, records the development of his art, the objects around his house and the meanings he attached to them.The collection includes photographs and records of individual works, among them the cement ball in his yard, The Devil and the Drunk Man, several untitled sculptures and his crucifixions. Some pieces are dated, including works from the 1930s, 1940s, 1950s and 1980s.The Smithsonian has also helped preserve and present the history of African American art and culture, though the supplied Souls Grown Deep profile does not establish that Hall's individual works are held in a Smithsonian collection. His documented legacy is firmly linked to the preservation work of Souls Grown Deep, which provides a record of the objects and the beliefs behind them.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: Bolivia declares state of emergency over El Nino weather pattern
articles.summary: Drought is affecting 78,000 families and has led to loss of over 75,000 cattle, as El Nino due to peak in late 2026.
articles.body:
Bolivia has declared a nationwide state of emergency to free up resources to deal with the effects of the El Nino weather phenomenon.

Bolivian President Rodrigo Paz signed the decree on Saturday, which also called for further deployments of rescue teams in areas of the country hard hit by flooding and drought.

El Nino will have “very severe impacts in terms of drought and floods”, Paz said, adding that Bolivia needs “the cooperation of all institutions”.

Drought is now affecting 78,000 families in six of Bolivia’s nine departments and has led to the loss of more than 75,000 cattle, according to a government report this week.

Bolivia is also prone to flooding. In December 2025, floods in the Santa Cruz region killed dozens of people.

Neighbouring Chile’s capital, Santiago, recorded the rainiest October ever, while wildfires in Peru killed at least 12 people last month.

El Nino, a global climate phenomenon that occurs roughly every two to seven years, is part of the planet’s natural weather cycle.

During this climate event, warming in the Pacific Ocean brings worldwide changes in winds, pressure, and rainfall patterns, often causing extreme weather.

El Nino’s intensity varies, and its impact changes based on geographic location, but this cycle could be the strongest in recorded history . It is due to peak at the end of 2026, but its impacts could continue well into 2027.

Scientists predict El Nino could cause more than 450,000 deaths globally , with the poorest countries worst impacted.

In early September, the World Meteorological Organization reported a nearly 100 percent likelihood that El Nino will continue through February 2027.
